times and which alone makes any time decisive, which alone
makes any time a genuine beginning or ending, an ultimate
turning point.
II
Nevertheless, it is sensible to look for a particular word of
Scripture; for the one word is enshrined in many forms. And
if this evening we seek such a word—we who are specially
conscious now of the passing of time-then let it be a word
which assures us, whose time is now fading away, of eternity
lying above and beyond time; let it be a word which will
bring the peace of God into the dispeace and agitation of our
human time. Let us listen to the farewell words of Jesus to
His disciples:
"Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the
world gives, give I to you. Let not your hearts be troubled,
neither let them be afraid" (John 14: 27).
It is peace which we need, peace which gives us the certitude
that we are not delivered over to the irresistible sweep of
time but are already integrally rooted in eternity. But it is
the peace of the Lord which the world cannot give; His
peace which is essentially other than all contentment which
the world can give. And does not the end of the term make
us acutely aware that we need this peace?
There is a pagan meditation for evening which we might
like to remember at this evening hour too:
"Let not sleep sink on tired eyelids without giving a
thought to each of the day's deeds. Where have I failed?
What have I done? What has remained undone? Thus
search your heart honestly. And then you may repent of
what you have done amiss, and rejoice in what you have
done well."
Who could deny that such meditation would be proper for
each one of us at the close of this term? Ought we not to
reflect on what we have achieved and what we have failed
to achieve? on the opportunities which the term has brought
us and which we have used and turned to good account-
